objectives.statement: Recognise a conditional probability from phrases such as 'given that', 'if' or 'of those who'.
Find conditional probabilities from a two-way table, a Venn diagram or a tree diagram.
Explain why $P(A\text{ given }B)$ and $P(B\text{ given }A)$ are usually different, and calculate a 'working backwards' conditional probability from a tree diagram.
Use conditional probability to decide whether two events are independent.

prerequisites.statement: Complete and read a two-set Venn diagram and a simple frequency table, including finding an 'only' region from a circle's total and the overlap (Lessons 8.1 and 8.3).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every conditional probability in this lesson is read from a DENOMINATOR GROUP inside a table or Venn diagram (a row, a column, a circle); without being able to read that group's total accurately first, there is nothing to divide by.

prerequisites.statement: Draw and use a tree diagram with and without replacement, multiplying along branches and adding across paths (Lesson 8.3).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A tree diagram's SECOND-STAGE branches are themselves conditional probabilities, and 'working backwards' on a tree (finding a probability about the first stage from information about the second) is the central new skill of this lesson, built directly on Lesson 8.3's tree method.

prerequisites.statement: Divide one fraction by another, and simplify the result.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The general conditional-probability formula $P(A\text{ given }B)=\dfrac{P(A\text{ and }B)}{P(B)}$ is itself a division of two fractions, and every 'working backwards' tree calculation ends in dividing one path's probability by a sum of several.

prerequisites.statement: Use the addition rule $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$ and recognise independent events as $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\times P(B)$ (Lesson 8.3).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Deciding independence in this lesson means comparing a conditional probability to an ordinary one, which only makes sense once the learner already has a firm, exact notion of what $P(A\cap B)$ and independence mean numerically.

diagnostic_items.question: In one sentence, what does 'given that' do to the sample space?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: It restricts the sample space to just the outcomes where the condition holds; that smaller number becomes the new total (denominator) for every probability calculated afterwards.

common_wrong_answers.answer: It just adds some extra information that makes the question harder, but the calculation is the same.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Fails to see 'given that' as changing WHICH number is used as the denominator; treats it as decorative context rather than as an instruction to shrink the sample space.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Tests the single idea the entire lesson is built on, before any specific diagram (table, Venn, tree) is involved.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Take a simple die example: 'P(6)' uses all 6 faces as the denominator, but 'P(6 given the score is even)' uses only the 3 even faces — physically cross out the odd faces to show the smaller world.

diagnostic_items.question: Why are $P(\text{rain given late})$ and $P(\text{late given rain})$ different in the train example?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: They use different denominators: $P(\text{late given rain})$ divides by the number of RAINY days, while $P(\text{rain given late})$ divides by the number of LATE trains; their numerators happen to be the same joint probability, but the totals they are compared against are not.

common_wrong_answers.answer: They shouldn't be different — if one is known the other must be the same value, just written the other way round.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Assumes conditional probability is symmetric (reversible) in the same way that, say, 'A is next to B' implies 'B is next to A', rather than recognising the two quantities are built from genuinely different groups.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This is the most commonly mis-remembered fact in the whole topic, so it is tested directly and early, using the lesson's own worked example as the reference case.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Write both fractions out in full with their actual numerators and denominators side by side (e.g. $\tfrac{0.12}{0.3}$ versus $\tfrac{0.12}{0.19}$) so the SAME numerator over two DIFFERENT denominators is visible.

diagnostic_items.question: A tree branch on the second stage reads $\tfrac49$. Is it a conditional probability? Explain.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Yes. It is the probability that the second draw gives a particular colour, GIVEN what was removed on the first draw — every second-stage branch on a tree diagram is a conditional probability, even though it is usually just written as a plain fraction.

common_wrong_answers.answer: No, it's just a fraction worked out from how many counters are left; conditional probability only applies when the question uses the words 'given that'.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Treats 'conditional probability' as a special labelled category of question rather than as a mathematical structure that a tree diagram's later branches ALWAYS have, whether or not the word 'given' ever appears.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks whether the learner can recognise conditional probability as a STRUCTURE (a probability calculated in a restricted situation) rather than only as a type of question explicitly flagged with the word 'given'.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Point to a specific second-stage branch on an already-drawn tree and ask 'what had to happen for us to even be looking at this branch?' — the answer is exactly the condition.

diagnostic_items.question: How can you tell from a table whether two events are independent?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Check whether the conditional probability of one event is the SAME across every category of the other (e.g. $P(\text{bus given Year 10})=P(\text{bus given Year 11})=P(\text{bus overall})$); if every row/column gives the same proportion, the events are independent.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Check that the numbers in the table are roughly similar across the rows.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Substitutes an eyeballed, approximate comparison of raw counts (which can differ hugely between rows just because the rows have different totals) for the correct comparison of PROPORTIONS (conditional probabilities), which is the only comparison that is actually meaningful.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Tests the practical, table-based version of the independence idea, directly setting up the related idea (false independence from similar-looking but unequal numbers).
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Calculate the exact conditional probability for each row as a fraction, cancel each to lowest terms, and only THEN compare them — never compare the raw frequencies directly.

theory_blocks.title: A conditional probability is probability in a smaller world
theory_blocks.body:
A conditional probability is an ordinary probability calculated in a *smaller world*. The condition tells you which group to look at, and that group becomes the new total (the denominator); everything else is counting inside it.

A fair die is thrown. $P(6)=\tfrac16$ normally. But told the score is *even*, the possible scores shrink to $2,4,6$ only, and one of those three is a $6$, so [[green:$P(6\text{ given even})=\tfrac13$]] — a genuinely different, larger probability, calculated inside a genuinely smaller world.

theory_blocks.title: Conditional probability: counting version
theory_blocks.body:
The **conditional probability** of $A$ given $B$ is the probability that $A$ happens when it is already known that $B$ has happened. Counting equally likely outcomes,
$$P(A\text{ given }B)=\frac{\text{number of outcomes in both }A\text{ and }B}{\text{number of outcomes in }B}.$$
The syllabus does not require the notation $P(A\mid B)$; in words, ‘given that’ is enough.

theory_blocks.title: The same rule, in probabilities
theory_blocks.body:
For events that are not equally-likely-outcome counts (for example, branches of a tree), the same rule works with probabilities instead of raw counts:
$$P(A\text{ given }B)=\frac{P(A\text{ and }B)}{P(B)}.$$
This single formula explains every method in this lesson: ‘both’ on top, the ‘given’ event's own probability underneath. You will not be asked to quote this formula in the exam (the syllabus does not require it), but it is the reason every table, Venn and tree method works.

theory_blocks.title: Two errors that undo a conditional probability
theory_blocks.body:
- Using the WHOLE population as the denominator. In ‘given that she is a girl’, the denominator is [[blue:the number of girls]], not [[red:the number of students]].
- Reversing the condition. The probability that a driver is a woman *given that* the driver is in an accident is NOT the same as the probability that a person has an accident *given that* she is a woman.

theory_blocks.title: Conditional probability from two-way tables
theory_blocks.body:
A two-way table classifies the same group in two ways. Here $100$ students are sorted by gender and by how they travel to school:

| | Walk | Bus | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Boys | $27$ | $18$ | $45$ |
| Girls | $22$ | $33$ | $55$ |
| Total | $49$ | $51$ | $100$ |

The row and column TOTALS are exactly the denominators a conditional probability needs: restrict to a row (or column), then read off the entry for the other event.

theory_blocks.title: Method for a two-way table
theory_blocks.body:
1. Decide which event is the CONDITION (the words after ‘given that’ or ‘of the’).
2. Go to that row or column and use ITS TOTAL as the denominator.
3. The numerator is the entry in that same row or column for the OTHER event.

theory_blocks.title: Conditional probability from Venn diagrams
theory_blocks.body: A Venn diagram is a two-way table drawn as circles. The condition is a WHOLE CIRCLE (or the region outside it), and the answer is the part of it lying in the other set. Of $40$ people: $16$ like rock only, $6$ like both, $12$ like jazz only, $6$ like neither.

assets.caption: All 40 people: 16 like rock only, 6 like both, 12 like jazz only, and 6 (outside both circles) like neither.
assets.purpose: Show the condition circle (e.g. 'likes jazz' = 6+12 = 18 people) and the region outside the rock circle (12+6 = 18 people) as concrete groups to restrict attention to, matching the related idea(a) and (b).

theory_blocks.title: A running check on a conditional-probability answer
theory_blocks.body: After choosing a denominator, check that the answer is a FRACTION OF THE CONDITION GROUP: the numerator can never be bigger than the denominator, and it must lie inside the condition circle (or row/column). If the numerator is drawn from a region OUTSIDE the condition, the calculation is wrong.

theory_blocks.title: Tree diagrams: second-stage branches are conditional
theory_blocks.body:
Tree diagrams give the probabilities of the SECOND stage GIVEN the first stage directly on the branches themselves. For a question in reverse (finding the FIRST stage given the second), the different paths that lead to the given outcome must be added together first.

Whether a train is late depends on the weather. $P(\text{rain})=0.3$. If it rains, the train is late with probability $0.4$; if dry, with probability $0.1$. The second-stage branches ($0.4$, $0.6$, $0.1$, $0.9$) ARE conditional probabilities: $0.4$ is $P(\text{late given rain})$.

assets.caption: Rain/late tree: second-stage branches 0.4/0.6/0.1/0.9 are themselves conditional probabilities.
assets.purpose: Show the second-stage branches are conditional probabilities before any 'working backwards' calculation is attempted, matching the related idea.

theory_blocks.title: Without replacement: reversing the order
theory_blocks.body:
Conditional probabilities appear naturally when items are not replaced. A bag has $6$ red and $4$ blue counters; two are taken without replacement. $P(\text{second blue given first red})=\tfrac49$ is read DIRECTLY off the branch, since after a red is removed, $9$ counters remain, $4$ of them blue.

The REVERSE question — $P(\text{first red given second blue})$ — cannot be read off a single branch: it needs every path where the second counter is blue (RB and BB) added together as the denominator.

assets.caption: 6 red, 4 blue, without replacement: second-stage branches read conditional probabilities directly; the reverse question needs paths added.
assets.purpose: Give a second concrete tree for both a forward (direct branch) and backward (added-paths) conditional probability, matching the related idea.

theory_blocks.title: Strategy for a conditional probability on a tree
theory_blocks.body:
1. Mark all paths where the GIVEN event occurs and add their probabilities; this is the denominator.
2. Of those, pick the paths where the OTHER event also occurs and add their probabilities; this is the numerator.
3. If the given event is the FIRST stage, the answer is simply the second-stage branch — no adding is needed at all.

theory_blocks.title: Conditional probability and independence
theory_blocks.body:
Two events are **independent** if knowing one has happened does not change the probability of the other — that is, the conditional probability EQUALS the ordinary (unconditional) probability:
$$A,B\text{ independent}\iff P(A\text{ given }B)=P(A).$$
In a school of $70$ Year 10 and $50$ Year 11 pupils, $28$ of the Year 10s and $20$ of the Year 11s travel by bus: $P(\text{bus given Year 10})=\tfrac{28}{70}=0.4$ and $P(\text{bus given Year 11})=\tfrac{20}{50}=0.4$, both equal to the overall $P(\text{bus})=\tfrac{48}{120}=0.4$ — so travelling by bus IS independent of year group here.

theory_blocks.title: Don't eyeball independence — compare exact fractions
theory_blocks.body: In the boys/girls travel table, $P(\text{walk})=0.49$ but $P(\text{walk given girl})=0.4$. They differ, so walking and gender are NOT independent in that sample. Do not conclude independence from one comparison of SIMILAR-LOOKING rounded numbers: always compare exact fractions (or test $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\times P(B)$ precisely).

keywords.definition: The probability that an event happens, given that another event is already known to have happened.
The event that restricts the sample space; it becomes the new denominator for every probability calculated afterwards.
A table classifying the same group by two different properties at once, with row and column totals.
The subset of the sample space picked out by the condition; its size is the conditional probability's denominator.
Finding a probability about an EARLIER stage from information about a LATER one, by adding every path that matches the later information.
Events where $P(A\text{ given }B)=P(A)$, so knowing one has happened does not change the probability of the other.
The count or probability of BOTH events happening together.
The count or probability of the CONDITION event alone — never the whole original population.
A branch on a tree diagram's second stage; its value is always a conditional probability, given the first-stage outcome.

worked_examples.statement: Reading a two-way table. One of the $100$ students in the travel table above is chosen at random. Find (a) the probability that the student walks; (b) the probability that the student walks, given that she is a girl; (c) the probability that the student is a girl, given that the student takes the bus.
reasoning: (a) has no condition, so the denominator is the full 100.
(b)'s condition is 'she is a girl', so the denominator is the GIRLS' ROW TOTAL (55), not 100.
(c)'s condition is 'takes the bus', so the denominator is the BUS COLUMN TOTAL (51), not 100.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $\tfrac{49}{100}$. (b) Restricting to the girls' row ($55$ students), $22$ walk: $\tfrac{22}{55}=\tfrac25$. (c) Restricting to the bus column ($51$ students), $33$ are girls: $\tfrac{33}{51}=\tfrac{11}{17}$. Notice (b) and (c) use different denominators ($55$ and $51$) and give different answers.
worked_examples.interpretation: Parts (a), (b) and (c) use the same table but three different denominators ($100$, the girls' row total $55$ and the bus column total $51$): the condition decides which group you divide by — this is the single idea the whole lesson turns on.
worked_examples.common_mistake: In (b), dividing by $100$ (the whole table) instead of $55$ (the girls' row total) — exactly the slip the related idea describes.

worked_examples.statement: Conditional probability from a Venn diagram. A person is chosen at random from the $40$ people above (16 rock only, 6 both, 12 jazz only, 6 neither). Find the probability that the person (a) likes rock, given that they like jazz; (b) likes jazz, given that they do *not* like rock.
reasoning: (a)'s condition 'likes jazz' is the WHOLE jazz circle: 6 (both) + 12 (jazz only) = 18 people.
(b)'s condition 'does not like rock' is everything OUTSIDE the rock circle: 12 (jazz only) + 6 (neither) = 18 people (coincidentally also 18, but a different group of people).
worked_examples.solution: (a) Jazz circle $=6+12=18$ people; of these, $6$ also like rock: $P=\tfrac6{18}=\tfrac13$. (b) Not-rock $=12+6=18$ people; of these, $12$ like jazz: $P=\tfrac{12}{18}=\tfrac23$. Compare with the UNCONDITIONAL $P(\text{rock})=\tfrac{22}{40}=0.55$: among jazz fans only $\tfrac13$ like rock, so liking jazz clearly changes the probability of liking rock — the two tastes are NOT independent.
worked_examples.interpretation: Even though both conditions happen to restrict to groups of the same SIZE (18 people), they are different groups of actual people, which is why (a) and (b) give different answers despite the same-looking denominator.
worked_examples.common_mistake: In (b), using the rock circle (22 people) as the denominator instead of everyone OUTSIDE it (18 people) — 'does not like rock' means the complement of the rock circle, not the circle itself.

worked_examples.statement: Working backwards. Using the rain/late tree above, find (a) the probability that the train is late; (b) the probability that it rained, given that the train was late.
knowns: P(late given rain)=0.4, P(late given dry)=0.1
reasoning: (a) 'Late' happens on two paths (rain-then-late, dry-then-late): add their probabilities.
(b) The denominator is EVERY path where the train is late (from part (a)); the numerator is only the RAIN-and-late path.
worked_examples.solution: (a) Late happens on two paths: $0.12+0.07=0.19$. (b) Restrict to the late paths only; their total probability is $0.19$, and $0.12$ of it belongs to the rain path: $P(\text{rain given late})=\dfrac{0.12}{0.19}=\dfrac{12}{19}\approx0.632$. Even though rain is only $0.3$ likely overall, more than half of all late trains occur on rainy days.
worked_examples.interpretation: Part (b) cannot be read off a single branch the way a FORWARD conditional probability can — it genuinely needs part (a)'s total as its denominator, which is exactly why 'working backwards' is harder than reading a branch directly.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Writing $P(\text{rain given late})=0.4$ (confusing it with $P(\text{late given rain})$, which IS a direct branch) instead of calculating the reverse quantity properly.

worked_examples.statement: Reversing the order. Use the $6$ red/$4$ blue tree above. Find (a) the probability that the second counter is blue, given that the first was red; (b) the probability that the first counter was red, given that the second is blue.
reasoning: (a) is a FORWARD question: the condition (first red) is the first stage, so the answer is simply the next branch.
(b) is a BACKWARD question: 'second is blue' can happen via RB or BB, so both paths must be added for the denominator, and only RB contributes to the numerator.
worked_examples.solution: (a) Read directly off the branch: after a red is removed, $9$ counters remain, $4$ of them blue: $\tfrac49$. (b) The second counter is blue on paths RB and BB: $\tfrac{24}{90}+\tfrac{12}{90}=\tfrac{36}{90}$. Of this, RB contributes $\tfrac{24}{90}$: $P(\text{first red given second blue})=\dfrac{24/90}{36/90}=\dfrac{24}{36}=\dfrac23$.
worked_examples.interpretation: (a) and (b) use the exact same four path-probabilities, but (a) needs only one of them (no addition at all) while (b) needs two of them (RB and BB) added for the denominator, with RB also as the numerator — the DIRECTION of the question entirely determines how much adding is required.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Answering (b) with $\tfrac6{10}$ (the UNCONDITIONAL probability the first counter was red), ignoring that the question is now restricted to the paths where the SECOND counter is blue.

worked_examples.statement: Are the events independent? In a school, $70$ pupils are in Year 10 and $50$ in Year 11. Of the Year 10 pupils, $28$ come by bus; of the Year 11 pupils, $20$ come by bus. Is travelling by bus independent of the year group?
reasoning: Calculate the conditional probability of 'bus' for EACH year group separately.
Compare both conditional probabilities to each other, and to the OVERALL probability of 'bus' across the whole school.
worked_examples.solution: $P(\text{bus given Year 10})=\tfrac{28}{70}=0.4$ and $P(\text{bus given Year 11})=\tfrac{20}{50}=0.4$. Overall, $P(\text{bus})=\tfrac{48}{120}=0.4$. The probability is unchanged whichever year group is looked at, so the events ARE independent.
worked_examples.interpretation: All three probabilities — both conditional ones and the overall one — must be compared as EXACT values (here, conveniently, all exactly $0.4$); this is the positive case that the related idea's caveat (don't eyeball similar-looking numbers) is contrasted against.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Comparing the raw COUNTS ($28$ vs $20$) instead of the conditional PROBABILITIES ($\tfrac{28}{70}$ vs $\tfrac{20}{50}$), and wrongly concluding the groups behave differently just because $28\ne20$.

guided_exercises.statement: $80$ students are sorted by gender and lunch choice: boys — canteen $24$, packed lunch $16$ (total $40$); girls — canteen $30$, packed lunch $10$ (total $40$). A student is chosen at random. Find (a) $P(\text{packed lunch given girl})$; (b) $P(\text{boy given canteen})$.
hints: For (a), the condition 'girl' restricts you to the girls' row (total 40) — use that as the denominator, not 80.
For (b), the condition 'canteen' restricts you to the canteen COLUMN; add the boys' and girls' canteen numbers first to get that column's total.
guided_exercises.full_solution: (a) Girls' row total $=40$; packed-lunch girls $=10$: $\tfrac{10}{40}=\tfrac14$. (b) Canteen column total $=24+30=54$; boys in that column $=24$: $\tfrac{24}{54}=\tfrac49$.
common_errors: In (b), dividing by $80$ (the whole table) instead of $54$ (the canteen column total).

guided_exercises.statement: Of $50$ people: $20$ do dance only, $10$ do both dance and yoga, $8$ do yoga only, and $12$ do neither. Find (a) $P(\text{dance given yoga})$; (b) $P(\text{yoga given not dance})$.
hints: For (a), the condition 'yoga' is the WHOLE yoga circle: add 'both' and 'yoga only' together for the denominator.
For (b), 'not dance' means everyone OUTSIDE the dance circle: add 'yoga only' and 'neither' together.
guided_exercises.full_solution: (a) Yoga circle $=10+8=18$; of these, $10$ also dance: $\tfrac{10}{18}=\tfrac59$. (b) Not-dance $=8+12=20$; of these, $8$ do yoga: $\tfrac8{20}=\tfrac25$.
common_errors: In (b), using the dance circle (30 people) as the denominator instead of everyone OUTSIDE it (20 people).

guided_exercises.statement: A bag has $5$ red and $3$ green counters. Two are taken without replacement. Find (a) $P(\text{second green given first red})$; (b) $P(\text{first green given second red})$.
hints: (a) is a FORWARD question — the condition is the first stage, so the answer is a single branch.
(b) is a BACKWARD question — 'second is red' happens on two paths (RR and GR); you need both of them for the denominator.
guided_exercises.full_solution: (a) After a red is removed, $7$ counters remain, $3$ of them green: $\tfrac37$. (b) $P(RR)=\tfrac58\times\tfrac47=\tfrac{20}{56}$; $P(GR)=\tfrac38\times\tfrac57=\tfrac{15}{56}$; $P(\text{second red})=\tfrac{35}{56}$. $P(\text{first green given second red})=\dfrac{15/56}{35/56}=\dfrac{15}{35}=\tfrac37$.
common_errors: In (b), answering with the unconditional $\tfrac38$ (the original probability the first was green) instead of restricting to paths where the SECOND counter is red.

exercises.statement: Complete the table for a class of $60$ (boys: pet $15$, total $28$; girls: total $32$; pet total $36$), and find the probability that a pupil chosen at random (a) is a girl, given that the pupil has a pet; (b) has no pet, given that the pupil is a boy.
exercises.full_solution: Boys no-pet $=28-15=13$; girls with pet $=36-15=21$; girls no-pet $=32-21=11$ (no-pet total $=24$). (a) $\tfrac{21}{36}=\tfrac7{12}$. (b) $\tfrac{13}{28}$.
common_errors: In (a), dividing by $60$ (the whole class) instead of $36$ (the pet-total, the condition group).

exercises.statement: A fair die is thrown. Given that the score is greater than $2$, find the probability that it is (a) a $5$; (b) even.
exercises.full_solution: Scores greater than $2$: $3,4,5,6$ ($4$ outcomes, the new denominator). (a) One of them is $5$: $\tfrac14$. (b) Even scores among them: $4,6$: $\tfrac24=\tfrac12$.
common_errors: Using $6$ (the original number of die faces) as the denominator instead of $4$ (the number of faces satisfying the condition).

exercises.statement: The table shows how $120$ pupils travel to school: Year 10 — bus $28$, walk $42$; Year 11 — bus $20$, walk $30$. One pupil is chosen at random. Find the probability that the pupil (a) takes the bus, given that the pupil is in Year 11; (b) is in Year 10, given that the pupil walks; (c) walks, given that the pupil is in Year 10.
common_errors: Confusing (a) and (c): (a) restricts to Year 11 and asks about bus; (c) restricts to Year 10 and asks about walking — using the wrong row/column total for either one.

exercises.statement: In a group of $50$ people, $30$ cycle, $25$ swim and $10$ do both; everyone does at least one of the two or neither. (a) Draw a Venn diagram. (b) Find the probability that a person swims, given that they cycle. (c) Find the probability that a person cycles, given that they swim.
exercises.full_solution: Cycle only $=30-10=20$, swim only $=25-10=15$, both $=10$, neither $=50-(20+10+15)=5$. (b) Cycle circle $=30$; swim-and-cycle $=10$: $\tfrac{10}{30}=\tfrac13$. (c) Swim circle $=25$; $\tfrac{10}{25}=\tfrac25$.
common_errors: Giving the same answer to (b) and (c) by assuming conditional probability is symmetric, instead of recalculating with the OTHER circle's total as the new denominator.

exercises.statement: A bag holds $5$ red and $3$ green counters. Two are taken without replacement. Find (a) $P(\text{second red given first red})$; (b) $P(\text{first green given second red})$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) After a red is removed, $4$ red remain out of $7$: $\tfrac47$. (b) $P(GR)=\tfrac38\times\tfrac57=\tfrac{15}{56}$; $P(\text{second red})=\tfrac{15}{56}+\tfrac{20}{56}=\tfrac{35}{56}$; answer $\tfrac{15}{35}=\tfrac37$.
common_errors: In (b), using $\tfrac38$ (the unconditional probability of green first) instead of restricting the denominator to paths where the SECOND counter is red.

exercises.statement: A factory has two machines. Machine A makes $60\%$ of the items and $2\%$ of them are defective; machine B makes $40\%$ and $5\%$ of them are defective. (a) Draw a tree diagram. (b) Find the probability that an item chosen at random is defective. (c) Given that an item is defective, find the probability that it was made by machine B.
common_errors: In (c), answering with $0.05$ (the $P(\text{defective given B})$ branch, a FORWARD conditional probability) instead of correctly working BACKWARDS from the defective total.

exercises.statement: Two fair dice are thrown. (a) Given that at least one die shows a $6$, find the probability that the total is $8$. (b) Given that the total is at least $10$, find the probability that the two scores are the same.
exercises.full_solution: (a) 'At least one 6': $11$ outcomes; of these, total $8$ occurs at $(2,6),(6,2)$: $\tfrac2{11}$. (b) 'Total $\ge10$': $(4,6),(6,4),(5,5),(5,6),(6,5),(6,6)$, $6$ outcomes; doubles among them: $(5,5),(6,6)$: $\tfrac26=\tfrac13$.
common_errors: In (a), using $36$ (the whole sample space) as the denominator instead of $11$ (the number of outcomes satisfying 'at least one 6').

exercises.statement: In a population of $1000$ people, $50$ have a condition. A test is positive for $45$ of those with the condition and for $95$ of those without it. A person tests positive. Find the probability that they have the condition. Explain why this is much lower than you might expect.
exercises.full_solution: Total positives $=45+95=140$. $\tfrac{45}{140}=\tfrac9{28}\approx0.321$. The condition is rare ($50$ out of $1000$), so even a fairly accurate test produces many FALSE positives from the large healthy population ($95$) that outnumber the true positives ($45$), pulling the conditional probability well below what the test's own accuracy might suggest.
common_errors: Answering with the test's accuracy on people WITH the condition ($\tfrac{45}{50}=0.9$) instead of working backwards from everyone who tested positive, healthy or not.

exercises.statement: The probability that it is dry is $0.7$. When it is dry, Tom wins his match with probability $0.6$; when it is wet, with probability $0.3$. Find the probability that Tom wins, and, given that he wins, the probability that it was dry.
common_errors: Answering the second part with $0.7$ (the unconditional $P(\text{dry})$) instead of restricting to the paths where Tom actually WINS.

exercises.statement: A sports club has $200$ members: $120$ adults and $80$ juniors. Of the adults, $45$ play tennis; of the juniors, $30$ play tennis. A member is chosen at random. (a) Find $P(\text{tennis given adult})$ and $P(\text{tennis given junior})$. (b) Find $P(\text{tennis})$ for the whole club. (c) Decide whether playing tennis is independent of being an adult, giving a reason.
exercises.answer: (a) $\tfrac{45}{120}=\tfrac38$ and $\tfrac{30}{80}=\tfrac38$ (b) $\tfrac{75}{200}=\tfrac38$ (c) Independent — both conditional probabilities equal the overall $P(\text{tennis})$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $P(\text{tennis given adult})=\tfrac{45}{120}=\tfrac38$ and $P(\text{tennis given junior})=\tfrac{30}{80}=\tfrac38$. (b) Tennis players $=45+30=75$, so $P(\text{tennis})=\tfrac{75}{200}=\tfrac38$. (c) Every one of these exact fractions is $\tfrac38$, so knowing that a member is an adult does not change the probability that they play tennis: the two events ARE independent. The product test agrees: $P(\text{adult})\times P(\text{tennis})=\tfrac{120}{200}\times\tfrac38=\tfrac{9}{40}$, and $P(\text{adult and tennis})=\tfrac{45}{200}=\tfrac{9}{40}$.
common_errors: Comparing the raw counts ($45$ adults against $30$ juniors) instead of the conditional probabilities $\tfrac{45}{120}$ and $\tfrac{30}{80}$, and concluding that the two groups behave differently when the proportions are identical.

exercises.statement: In a survey of $200$ people, $100$ are under the age of $30$ (the younger group) and $100$ are aged $30$ or over (the older group). Of the younger group, $42$ own a bicycle; of the older group, $39$ own a bicycle. A person is chosen at random. (a) Find $P(\text{bicycle given younger})$ and $P(\text{bicycle given older})$. (b) Find $P(\text{bicycle})$ for the whole survey. (c) A student says: 'both answers to (a) are about $0.4$, so owning a bicycle is independent of age group'. Explain why the student is wrong.
exercises.answer: (a) $\tfrac{42}{100}=0.42$ and $\tfrac{39}{100}=0.39$ (b) $\tfrac{81}{200}=0.405$ (c) Not independent — $0.42\ne0.39$, and neither equals $0.405$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $P(\text{bicycle given younger})=\tfrac{42}{100}=0.42$ and $P(\text{bicycle given older})=\tfrac{39}{100}=0.39$. (b) Bicycle owners $=42+39=81$, so $P(\text{bicycle})=\tfrac{81}{200}=0.405$. (c) Independence is an EXACT equality, not a rough resemblance: $0.42\ne0.39$, and neither of them equals the overall $0.405$, so knowing which age group a person is in DOES change the probability that they own a bicycle. The product test gives the same verdict: $P(\text{younger})\times P(\text{bicycle})=\tfrac12\times\tfrac{81}{200}=\tfrac{81}{400}=0.2025$, but $P(\text{younger and bicycle})=\tfrac{42}{200}=0.21$.
common_errors: Judging independence by eye from decimals that look alike ($0.42$ and $0.39$ are both 'about $0.4$') instead of testing whether the exact values are equal.
Comparing the two conditional probabilities with each other but forgetting to check them against the overall $P(\text{bicycle})=0.405$.

exam_questions.statement:
The table shows how $90$ members of a gym prefer to train.

| | Weights | Cardio | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Men | $24$ | $16$ | $40$ |
| Women | $18$ | $32$ | $50$ |
| Total | $42$ | $48$ | $90$ |

A member is chosen at random.
(a) Find the probability that the member prefers cardio. [1]
(b) Find the probability that the member prefers weights, given that the member is a woman. [2]
(c) Find the probability that the member is a man, given that the member prefers cardio. [2]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $\tfrac{48}{90}=\tfrac8{15}$. (b) Women's row total $=50$; weights among women $=18$: $\tfrac{18}{50}=\tfrac9{25}$. (c) Cardio column total $=48$; men in that column $=16$: $\tfrac{16}{48}=\tfrac13$.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 for $\tfrac{48}{90}$ or $\tfrac8{15}$ or an equivalent decimal/percentage
(b) M1 for identifying the women's row total (50) as the denominator; A1 for $\tfrac{18}{50}$ or $\tfrac9{25}$
(c) M1 for identifying the cardio column total (48) as the denominator; A1 for $\tfrac{16}{48}$ or $\tfrac13$.
common_errors: In (b) and (c), dividing by $90$ (the grand total) instead of the relevant row/column total, losing the method mark in each part even if the numerator is correct.

exam_questions.statement:
Of $60$ students, $25$ study Physics only, $15$ study both Physics and Chemistry, $12$ study Chemistry only, and $8$ study neither.
(a) Find the probability that a student chosen at random studies Chemistry. [1]
(b) Find the probability that a student studies Physics, given that the student studies Chemistry. [2]
(c) Find the probability that a student studies Chemistry, given that the student does not study Physics. [2]
exam_questions.full_solution: Chemistry total $=15+12=27$. (a) $\tfrac{27}{60}=\tfrac9{20}$. (b) Chemistry circle $=27$; both $=15$: $\tfrac{15}{27}=\tfrac59$. (c) Not-Physics $=12+8=20$; Chemistry among them $=12$: $\tfrac{12}{20}=\tfrac35$.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 for $\tfrac{27}{60}$ or $\tfrac9{20}$
(b) M1 for using the Chemistry total (27) as the denominator; A1 for $\tfrac{15}{27}$ or $\tfrac59$
(c) M1 for using 'not Physics' (20) as the denominator, not the Physics circle; A1 for $\tfrac{12}{20}$ or $\tfrac35$.
common_errors: In (c), using the Physics circle (40 students) as the denominator instead of the $20$ students OUTSIDE it.

exam_questions.statement:
A factory has two machines. Machine A makes $55\%$ of the items produced, and $3\%$ of its items are defective. Machine B makes the remaining $45\%$, and $6\%$ of its items are defective.
(a) Draw a tree diagram to show this information. [2]
(b) Find the probability that an item chosen at random is defective. [2]
(c) Given that an item is defective, find the probability that it was made by machine B. [3]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) First-stage: A ($0.55$), B ($0.45$); second-stage: defective ($0.03$)/good ($0.97$) under A, defective ($0.06$)/good ($0.94$) under B. (b) $P(\text{defective})=0.55\times0.03+0.45\times0.06=0.0165+0.027=0.0435$. (c) $P(B\text{ given defective})=\dfrac{0.027}{0.0435}=\dfrac{18}{29}\approx0.621$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for correct first-stage branches (0.55, 0.45); M1 for correct second-stage branches (0.03/0.97 and 0.06/0.94)
(c) M1 for identifying $0.45\times0.06$ as the numerator; M1 for dividing by their (b); A1 for $\tfrac{18}{29}$ or $0.621$ (3 s.f.).
common_errors: In (c), dividing $0.06$ by $0.0435$ (using the BRANCH value instead of the full joint probability $0.45\times0.06=0.027$ as the numerator).

challenge_questions.statement: A bag holds $3$ red and $2$ blue counters. Two are taken without replacement. Given that at least one is red, find the probability that both are red.
challenge_questions.full_solution: $P(RR)=\tfrac35\times\tfrac24=\tfrac3{10}$. $P(\text{at least one red})=1-P(BB)=1-\tfrac1{10}=\tfrac9{10}$. $P(\text{both red given at least one red})=\dfrac{3/10}{9/10}=\dfrac13$.

challenge_questions.statement: Three fair coins are tossed. Given that at least one is a head, find the probability that at least two are heads.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Of the $8$ equally likely outcomes, $7$ have at least one head (all except TTT). Of those $7$, $4$ have at least two heads: HHH, HHT, HTH, THH. $P=\dfrac47$.

challenge_questions.statement: A bag holds $3$ white and $x$ black counters. Two are taken without replacement and $P(\text{both white})=\tfrac3{10}$. Show that $x^2+5x-14=0$, find $x$ and hence the probability that the second counter is white, given that the first was white.
challenge_questions.full_solution: $\dfrac{3}{3+x}\times\dfrac{2}{2+x}=\dfrac3{10}\Rightarrow60=3(x+3)(x+2)\Rightarrow20=x^2+5x+6\Rightarrow x^2+5x-14=0$. Factorising, $(x+7)(x-2)=0$, so $x=2$ (rejecting the negative root). With $x=2$, after one white is removed, $2$ white remain among $3+2-1=4$: $\tfrac24=\tfrac12$.

challenge_questions.statement: Two events $A$ and $B$ satisfy $P(A)=0.5$, $P(B)=0.4$ and $P(\text{both})=0.2$. Show that $A$ and $B$ are independent. If instead $P(\text{both})=0.3$, find $P(A\text{ given }B)$ and $P(B\text{ given }A)$, and explain why they differ.
challenge_questions.full_solution: $0.5\times0.4=0.2=P(\text{both})$, so $A$ and $B$ are independent. With $P(\text{both})=0.3$: $P(A\text{ given }B)=\tfrac{0.3}{0.4}=0.75$ and $P(B\text{ given }A)=\tfrac{0.3}{0.5}=0.6$; they differ because the two conditional probabilities divide the SAME joint probability ($0.3$) by two DIFFERENT denominators, $P(B)=0.4$ and $P(A)=0.5$.

challenge_questions.statement: In the tree diagram for the train, explain in words why $P(\text{rain given late})=\tfrac{12}{19}$ is bigger than $P(\text{rain})=0.3$, and calculate $P(\text{rain given on time})$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Rain makes lateness much more likely ($0.4$ against only $0.1$ when dry), so among ALL late trains, rainy days are heavily over-represented compared to their $0.3$ share of all days — which is exactly why conditioning on 'late' pushes the probability of rain up. $P(\text{on time})=0.18+0.63=0.81$; $P(\text{rain given on time})=\dfrac{0.18}{0.81}=\dfrac29\approx0.222$, which is BELOW $0.3$, the mirror image of the 'late' case.

mcq.stem: In a survey of $100$ people, $60$ own a car and $40$ do not. Of the car owners, $25$ are men. What is $P(\text{man given owns a car})$?

options.why_wrong: Uses the WHOLE population ($100$) as the denominator instead of the condition group (the $60$ car owners).
Divides by the number who do NOT own a car, the wrong condition group entirely.
This is $P(\text{owns a car})$, not $P(\text{man given owns a car})$.

mcq.explanation: The condition 'owns a car' restricts the denominator to the $60$ car owners; $25$ of them are men, so $P(\text{man given owns a car})=\tfrac{25}{60}=\tfrac5{12}$.

mcq.stem: In a school of $150$ students (80 boys, 70 girls), $16$ boys are left-handed, so $P(\text{left-handed given boy})=0.2$. There are $30$ left-handed students in total. What is $P(\text{boy given left-handed})$?

options.why_wrong: Assumes $P(\text{boy given left-handed})=P(\text{left-handed given boy})$, but the two use different denominators (left-handed total vs boys total).
This is $P(\text{girl given left-handed})$ ($30-16=14$ left-handed girls), not $P(\text{boy given left-handed})$.
Uses the WHOLE school as the denominator instead of restricting to the $30$ left-handed students.

mcq.explanation: Restricting to the $30$ left-handed students, $16$ of them are boys: $P(\text{boy given left-handed})=\tfrac{16}{30}=\tfrac8{15}$, a different value from $P(\text{left-handed given boy})=0.2$.

mcq.stem: $150$ students: $90$ in Year 10 (of whom $36$ take the bus) and $60$ in Year 11 (of whom $24$ take the bus). Is taking the bus independent of year group?

options.text: Yes — both year groups give exactly $P(\text{bus})=0.4$.
No — the raw counts ($36$ vs $24$) are different, so the groups must behave differently.
options.why_wrong: Compares raw COUNTS instead of the conditional PROBABILITIES; the counts differ only because the two year groups have different total sizes (90 vs 60), not because the proportions differ.

options.text: No — Year 10 has more students overall.
options.why_wrong: The total SIZE of a group is irrelevant to independence; only the PROPORTION taking the bus within each group matters.
This arithmetic fact has no connection to independence; the conclusion happens to be right but for a reason that is mathematically meaningless.

mcq.explanation: $P(\text{bus given Year 10})=\tfrac{36}{90}=0.4$ and $P(\text{bus given Year 11})=\tfrac{24}{60}=0.4$: both conditional probabilities are EXACTLY equal, so bus travel is independent of year group here.

mcq.stem: On a tree diagram for drawing two counters without replacement, a second-stage branch reads $\tfrac49$. What does this number represent?

options.text: The overall probability of that colour in the whole original bag
options.why_wrong: A second-stage branch reflects the bag AFTER the first counter was removed, not the original, unconditioned bag.

options.text: $P(\text{second counter is that colour, given what the first counter was})$

options.why_wrong: This describes a FIRST-stage branch, not a second-stage one; the two stages represent different draws.

options.text: An unconditional probability with no connection to the first draw
options.why_wrong: Every second-stage branch is conditioned on which first-stage branch was taken — it is never free-standing or unconnected.

mcq.explanation: Every second-stage branch on a tree diagram is exactly the probability of that stage's outcome, GIVEN the outcome of the stage before it — a conditional probability, whether or not the word 'given' appears.

mcq.stem: A train is late with probability $0.4$ when it rains ($P(\text{rain})=0.3$) and $0.1$ when dry. Given that the train is late, what is $P(\text{rain})$?

options.why_wrong: This is the UNCONDITIONAL $P(\text{rain})$, ignoring the extra information that the train was late.
This is $P(\text{late given rain})$, the FORWARD conditional probability — not the BACKWARD one asked for here.
This is the joint probability $P(\text{rain and late})$, the numerator only — it still needs to be divided by $P(\text{late})=0.19$.

mcq.explanation: $P(\text{rain and late})=0.3\times0.4=0.12$; $P(\text{late})=0.12+0.07=0.19$; $P(\text{rain given late})=\dfrac{0.12}{0.19}=\dfrac{12}{19}\approx0.632$.

flashcards.back: $P(A\text{ given }B)=\dfrac{\text{number of outcomes in both }A\text{ and }B}{\text{number of outcomes in }B}$

flashcards.front: Conditional probability (general version)
flashcards.back: $P(A\text{ given }B)=\dfrac{P(A\text{ and }B)}{P(B)}$ — works for any probabilities, not just equally-likely counts.

flashcards.front: True or false: 'given that she is a girl' means you still divide by the total number of students.
flashcards.back: False. The denominator becomes the number of GIRLS only — the condition shrinks the sample space before any counting happens.

flashcards.front: True or false: $P(A\text{ given }B)$ always equals $P(B\text{ given }A)$.
flashcards.back: False in general — they usually have different denominators ($B$'s total vs $A$'s total), even though they can share the same numerator.

flashcards.front: True or false: two conditional probabilities that look similar after rounding prove the events are independent.
flashcards.back: False. Independence is an EXACT equality; always compare exact fractions (or test $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\times P(B)$ precisely), not rounded decimals that merely look alike.

flashcards.front: Method for a two-way table conditional probability
flashcards.back: 1. Identify the CONDITION. 2. Use that row/column's TOTAL as the denominator. 3. Read the numerator from the SAME row/column.

flashcards.front: Method for a conditional probability on a tree diagram
flashcards.back: 1. Add the probabilities of every path where the GIVEN event occurs (denominator). 2. Of those, add the paths where the OTHER event also occurs (numerator). 3. If the given event is the FIRST stage, just read the branch directly.

flashcards.front: P(A given B) vs. P(B given A) — what's actually different?
flashcards.back: Both can share the same numerator (the 'both' probability), but they divide it by DIFFERENT denominators: $P(B)$ for one, $P(A)$ for the other.

flashcards.front: What does 'given that' do to a probability calculation?
flashcards.back: It restricts the sample space to just the outcomes satisfying the condition; that smaller group becomes the new total (denominator) for everything calculated afterwards.

flashcards.front: How do you test whether events $A$ and $B$ are independent, using conditional probability?
flashcards.back: Check whether $P(A\text{ given }B)=P(A)$ (equivalently $P(B\text{ given }A)=P(B)$, or $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\times P(B)$).

flashcards.front: Which phrases signal a conditional probability question?
flashcards.back: 'Given that...', 'if...', 'of those who...', 'of the [group]...' — all of them mean: restrict the denominator to that group first.

flashcards.front: Why is a tree diagram's second-stage branch already a conditional probability?
flashcards.back: It gives the probability of that stage's outcome GIVEN that a specific first-stage path was followed — the conditioning is built into the diagram's structure, even with no 'given' wording written anywhere.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: When finding a conditional probability, the denominator is always the size of the WHOLE population in the question, regardless of what the condition restricts attention to.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Every earlier probability calculation in the course (Lessons 8.1-8.3) used the whole sample space as the denominator, so it is a strong, well-practised habit to keep doing exactly that, even once a condition has been introduced that should shrink it.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: Given 'the probability that a student walks to school, given that she is a girl', the learner divides by the TOTAL number of students instead of by the number of GIRLS.
misconceptions.correct_model: The denominator of a conditional probability is the size of the CONDITION GROUP ONLY (e.g. the number of girls), never the whole population, because 'given that' has already restricted attention to that smaller group before any counting begins.
misconceptions.remediation: Before dividing anything, physically identify and count the condition group ON ITS OWN first (ignore everyone outside it completely), and only then count how many of THAT group also satisfy the other event.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: $P(A\text{ given }B)$ and $P(B\text{ given }A)$ must be the same value, since they both involve exactly the same two events $A$ and $B$.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The two phrases look almost like the same sentence with the words swapped, and in ordinary English swapping the order of a description ('a driver who is a woman' vs 'a woman who is a driver') often doesn't change its meaning much, which does not carry over to conditional probability.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner treats a given value of $P(A\text{ given }B)$ as automatically also equal to $P(B\text{ given }A)$, without recalculating using $B$'s total as the new denominator.
misconceptions.correct_model: $P(A\text{ given }B)$ and $P(B\text{ given }A)$ generally use DIFFERENT denominators ($B$'s total vs $A$'s total) even though they can share the same numerator (the 'both' count), so the two values are usually different and must be calculated separately.
misconceptions.remediation: Always write out which group is the denominator BEFORE calculating — state in words 'out of all the [condition group], how many also have [other property]?' — for each of the two conditional probabilities separately.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Two conditional probabilities that come out numerically CLOSE to each other (e.g. $0.42$ and $0.39$) are close enough to call the two events independent.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Real data from a sample rarely gives perfectly round, identical decimals, so after rounding, two genuinely different underlying proportions can look deceptively similar, and 'basically the same' feels like a reasonable standard for a judgement call.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner concludes 'independent' (or 'not independent') based on rounded decimals that look alike (or different), without comparing the EXACT fractions or explicitly testing $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\times P(B)$.
misconceptions.correct_model: Independence is an exact mathematical equality, not an approximate judgement: compare exact fractions (or test $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\times P(B)$ precisely) rather than rounded decimals that merely look alike.
misconceptions.remediation: Convert every relevant probability to an exact fraction in lowest terms before comparing them, and explicitly write out the equality (or inequality) being tested, rather than eyeballing rounded decimals.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A plain fraction written on the second set of branches of a tree diagram (e.g. $\tfrac49$) is just an ordinary, unconditional probability, not a conditional one, unless the question explicitly uses the word 'given'.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The branch is written as a bare number with no visible 'given that' wording attached to it, so it looks structurally identical to any other probability the learner has seen — the conditioning is implicit in the diagram's STRUCTURE (which branch you took to get there) rather than stated in words.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner cannot explain what a second-stage branch value actually represents, or treats it as if it applied to the WHOLE original bag rather than to the situation that exists after the first draw.
misconceptions.correct_model: Every second-stage branch on a tree diagram already IS a conditional probability — the probability of that outcome GIVEN that the path leading to it was followed — whether or not the word 'given' is written anywhere on the diagram.
misconceptions.remediation: For any second-stage branch, say out loud in full: 'this is the probability of [this outcome], GIVEN that [the first-stage outcome] already happened', before using the number in any calculation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Not checking that a conditional-probability numerator is genuinely INSIDE the chosen condition group before dividing.
common_mistakes.why: Once a number has been pulled from somewhere in a table or Venn diagram, it is easy to assume it belongs to the right region without explicitly checking it lies inside the group just restricted to.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Before dividing, state in words exactly which group the numerator is counted from, and confirm that group is entirely contained within the condition group used as the denominator.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing only a final decimal for a 'working backwards' tree calculation (e.g. '0.632') without showing the numerator and denominator separately.
common_mistakes.why: Once the final division has been done on a calculator, it feels like the working is already clear from the final number alone.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always write the calculation as an explicit fraction first, e.g. $\dfrac{0.12}{0.19}$, before giving the decimal — the fraction itself is where most of the method marks sit.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaving a conditional-probability fraction unsimplified (e.g. $\tfrac{24}{90}$ instead of $\tfrac4{15}$), or simplifying it incorrectly under time pressure.
common_mistakes.why: Conditional-probability fractions often come from adding several tree-diagram products first, and by the time that addition is finished, simplifying can feel like a final, skippable flourish.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Treat simplifying the final fraction as a required last step, exactly as with any other fractions question, and double-check the simplification by multiplying back up.

exam_notes: Conditional probability questions are usually set on a table, a Venn diagram or a tree with a short context. Command words 'given that', 'of these', 'if one is chosen from those who...' all signal a reduced denominator.
Leave answers as exact fractions (simplified) unless asked for a decimal; round a decimal answer to $3$ significant figures.

Show the numerator and the denominator SEPARATELY in a 'working backwards' tree calculation, e.g. $\dfrac{0.12}{0.12+0.07}$, before giving $\tfrac{12}{19}$: a correct final answer earns the marks, but if the answer is wrong, the method marks can only be given for working you have shown.

When asked to decide independence, compare EXACT fractions (or explicitly test $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\times P(B)$) rather than rounded decimals — a 'show that' independence question needs the equality demonstrated with exact values, not an approximate judgement.

summary.big_idea: A conditional probability is an ordinary probability calculated inside a SMALLER world: the condition picks out a group (a table row/column, a Venn circle, a set of tree paths), that group's own size becomes the new denominator, and $P(A\text{ given }B)$ almost always differs from $P(B\text{ given }A)$ because the two use different denominators.
key_points: $P(A\text{ given }B)=\dfrac{\text{outcomes (or probability) in both }A\text{ and }B}{\text{outcomes (or probability) in }B}$; the condition's own group is always the denominator, never the whole population.

Tables: use the condition's row/column total as the denominator. Venn diagrams: the condition is a whole circle (or outside it). Trees: add every path with the condition, then pick out the paths that also have the other event.
A tree's second-stage branches are already conditional probabilities on the first stage; a 'working backwards' question needs several paths added for its denominator, not just one branch read off.
$P(A\text{ given }B)\ne P(B\text{ given }A)$ in general, since they share a numerator but divide it by different denominators.
Events are independent exactly when $P(A\text{ given }B)=P(A)$; test this with EXACT fractions, never by eyeballing similar-looking rounded decimals.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Identify the CONDITION first, use its own group's size (row/column total, whole circle, or sum of matching tree paths) as the denominator — never the whole original population — and never assume $P(A\text{ given }B)$ equals $P(B\text{ given }A)$ without recalculating with the other denominator.
